meta.title: Under the Microscope: A Brief History of Microscopy
meta.author: William J Croft
meta.publisher: World Scientific Publishing Co. Pte. Ltd.

sentences: The **foreword** of "Under the Microscope" explores the history of humanity's fascination with the **"small world"**, from early magnifying lenses to modern sophisticated techniques.

The book covers the milestones in **microscopy**, including **van Leeuwenhoek's** high-resolution microscopes and the evolution of **optical** and **electron microscopes**, eventually leading to modern **scanning probe microscopy**.

It places significant emphasis on the increasing **magnification** and measurement units such as **microns** and **nanometers** used in today's high-tech **microscopes**, setting a context for the atomic-scale imaging.

parts.title: Pioneers of Early Microscopy: Hooke and Leeuwenhoek

sentences: **Robert Hooke** (1635-1703) was a pivotal figure in early **microscopy**.
Known for the book "Micrographia," he coined the term **"cells"** after observing the structure of **cork**.
Despite preferring **compound microscopes**, he acknowledged the clarity of **single lens instruments**.
Hooke made major contributions, including **Hooke's Law** of **elasticity** and early theories regarding the **wave nature** of light.
Another significant contributor was **Antony van Leeuwenhoek**, a **Dutch draper** (**1632-1723**).
Despite no formal education, he ground **microscope lenses** and made groundbreaking **biological observations**.
Leeuwenhoek discovered **bacteria**, **sperm cells**, and **blood cells**, contributing immensely to the field.
Notably, he built over **500 microscopes** and preferred single lens designs, contrary to Hooke's views.
In his interactions, Leeuwenhoek was known for his meticulous nature and maintained a strong relationship with the **Royal Society** in London.
His diverse work experience included roles such as **surveyor** and **wine assayer**.
Through dedication, he raised **scientific awareness** and his discoveries caught the attention of many contemporary **scientists**.
Known for meticulous methods, his exact surname's pronunciation remains a point of historic curiosity.

parts.title: Historical Foundations of Microscopy and Optics

paragraphs.heading: Summary of Key Points: Early Exploration of Light and Optics
sentences: Microscopy's **historical development** **began with the Ancient Greeks**.
It notes early observations such as **Aristophanes' mention of glass globules** in Athens and **Euclid's foundational work in optics**, around **300 B.C.**.
These figures laid the groundwork for understanding **light as a straight line** and the phenomenon of **refraction**, where light bends upon entering different media.

Important concepts like **refraction** are explained with visual aids: a stick appearing bent in water, and soldiers changing direction on uneven terrain, illustrating light's behavior as it travels through **different densities**.
The transition from low- to high-density media (e.g., air to glass) further explains **light bending** towards the surface.
**Curved surfaces on glass lead to lens formation**, demonstrating early understandings of **optics and magnification**.
The discovery of a **plano-convex lens at Nimrod** signifies early lens use, presumed to date back **to the 700s B.C.**, though initially thought to be more decorative than functional.
By the **first century A.D.**, individuals like **Seneca** discussed magnification through water globes.

Innovations like spectacles in **1280 Florence** amplified still-limited but intriguing **optical knowledge**, spreading quickly across the world while laying the foundations for more advanced studies.
Crystals have **periodically** arranged atoms, unlike **glasses** and **liquids** where atoms are **randomly** arranged.
This arrangement gives crystals unique **properties**.
The **"law of constancy of interfacial angles"** states that angles between similar crystal faces are **constant** for the same material.
Crystal properties come from their **internal structure**.
**Symmetry operations** like rotations and mirrors classify crystals into **six crystal systems** based on their **axes** and **angles**.
These systems include cubic, tetragonal, hexagonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, and triclinic.
Crystals have **axes**, **planes**, and a **center** of symmetry.
These elements lead to **32 point groups** that describe crystal **morphology**.
The repetition of the smallest structural unit fits into one of **14 Bravais lattices**, which describe the crystal's spatial arrangement.
**Polarizing microscopes** use **polarized light** to reveal crystal properties based on these **symmetries**.
Features like **anisotropy** or **isotropy** show how light interacts with crystals of different symmetry, enhancing **mineralogical**, **geological**, and **chemical** study today.

parts.title: Polarized Light and Crystal Properties Overview

paragraphs.heading: Polarized Light and Crystal Properties
sentences: In **crystals**, directional and **value properties** can be represented by **vector surfaces**.
For example, in **cubic crystals**, **thermal expansion** appears isotropic, forming a **sphere**.
However, in **lower symmetry** crystals like **hexagonal or tetragonal**, expansion forms a **revolution ellipsoid**.
The **optical properties**, such as the **velocity of light** in a crystal, have vector surfaces like a **sphere** in cubic crystals, making them **optically isotropic**.
**Non-cubic crystals** split light into two **polarized rays** — the **ordinary ray** (spherical vector surface) and the **extraordinary ray** (ellipsoid vector surface).

paragraphs.heading: Summary Chunk
sentences: **Light Microscopy**'s history is filled with **explorations** into both **transparent** and **opaque** materials.
While **biological materials** were initially more revealing, metals posed challenges due to their surface-level observations.

In **1664, Henry Power** documented **metal surfaces**, noting **irregularities** and **vitrification** of sparks, while **Robert Hooke** delved into this phenomenon in his famous **"Micrographia"** work.
Hooke's **compound microscope** observations nurtured the development of metal study, although his metallurgical insights were limited to external features like **scratches on a razor**.

paragraphs.heading: Metallurgical Advances
sentences: **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek**, known for his exploration of **microscopic world**, contributed to metals' study by identifying **crystalline structures** in **the 1700s**.
Later, **Henry Clifton Sorby**, in **1850**, advanced metal microscopy.
Despite limited initial awareness, Sorby refined **etching techniques** and identified **microstructures in steel**, laying foundational **metallurgical principles**.
His **polishing** and **magnification** methods were novel, serving as a **lens into metal's micro-world**.
Sorby's microscope **advancements** contributed significantly to metallurgy, underpinning modern techniques.

paragraphs.heading: Reflected Light and Scientific Developments
sentences: Through advances like **R. Beck's reflector** and **Lieberkuhn’s mirror**, greatly improved **microscopy of opaque structures** emerged.
Sorby’s use of **reflected light** techniques distinguished textures and compositions, critical for studying metals like **iron and steel**.

As science progressed, tools like **electron-probe micro-analyzers** provided refined ways to analyze opaque minerals, aligned with observed **optical properties** like **brightness** and **hardness**.
This led to broader applications in **Materials Science** and **Forensic Science**, revealing the depth and **complexity of the microstructures** in **metallurgical and other scientific fields**.
Electron microscopy has many contributors, with **Max Knoll** and **Ernst Ruska** making notable progress in **1931**.
They built a **magnetic lens** microscope, leading to advancements in electron microscope development.
**Günther Rüdenberg** filed a patent for the electron microscope using multiple lenses the same year.

The electron microscope's capability to see below atomic levels stems from electrons' **small size** compared to atoms, with techniques like **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)** enhancing this ability.
**Electron guns** and **magnetic lenses** form the core of the electron microscope, which captures images through fluorescent materials.

parts.title: Electron Diffraction and its Historical Development

sentences: **Electron diffraction** is a powerful method used in **electron microscopes** to study the properties and structure of **crystals**.

It builds upon Max von Laue's discovery of X-ray diffraction in 1912, showing that crystals can diffract X-rays and electrons into a **periodic pattern**, helping identify materials and their characteristics.

In 1912, von Laue received a **Nobel Prize** for his work, which was further simplified by **W.H. Bragg** using Bragg's Law, allowing for the precise calculation of crystal structure based on the diffraction pattern.

parts.title: Chemical Composition Analysis via Microscopy Techniques

sentences: **Optical Microscopy** uses **polarized light** for analyzing chemical **composition** of small samples, like in forensic or materials science.
This technique, once widespread, is becoming obsolete due to the rise of instruments like the **Electron Probe Microanalyser (EPMA)**, which enable precise analysis at higher costs.
Unfortunately, **optical methods** are no longer commonly taught in universities, except in certain institutes like the **McCrone Institute of Chicago**.
**X-Rays and Electrons**: The basics of the **X-Ray process** began with Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen's discovery, leading to the identification of different **radiation types** like K and L by Barkla.

Later, the diffraction works by Max von Laue, and significant contributions by W. H. Bragg, and his son, confirmed the periodic nature of atoms and led to the development of **X-ray spectrographs** for material analysis.
**Henry Moseley** revolutionized understanding atomic numbers through his X-ray spectrometry work with elements.
**Early X-ray Discoveries**: Moseley's studies proved the **periodic table's** completeness and helped predict new elements.

His pioneering work was cut short due to his early death in World War I. **EPMA Development**: Raymond Castaing developed the **first microprobe** for **chemical analysis** by modifying an electron microscope.
Castaing detailed how localized analysis was possible by focusing an **electron beam** and measuring **secondary X-rays**.
Despite its age, this technique strikes a balance between **cost and efficacy** for detailed compositional analysis.

parts.title: Atomic-Level Microscopic Techniques in Modern Studies

paragraphs.heading: Quantum Microscopy and Molecule Imaging
sentences: The **Scannning Probe Microscopes (SPM)**, including the **Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM)**, revolutionized microscopy by allowing visualization at an **atomic level**.
The STM achieves this through an **atomically sharp probe** and quantum tunneling, overcoming limitations of traditional microscopes.
Several issues such as vibration isolation, probe sharpening, and precise scanning movements were ingeniously addressed, which allowed visualization of the **atomic arrangement on surfaces**.

paragraphs.heading: Atomic Force and New Measurement Modes
sentences: The **Atomic Force Microscope (AFM)** emerged as a derivative of the STM, enabling study of **non-conductive surfaces**.
AFM uses an ultra-sharp tip to scan the surface topography and operates in **contact or tapping modes**.
It's employed in varied environments including **liquid**, making it useful for biological samples.
Besides topography, AFM supports techniques like **Lateral Force Microscopy** or **Chemical Force Microscopy**, which investigate **frictional forces and molecular interactions**.

paragraphs.heading: Biofilms and Advanced Imaging Techniques
sentences: **Confocal Microscopy** solved the limitations of scattering by employing a confocal setup for better depth resolution, revealing structures like **biofilms** in detail.
It aids in studies like drug effect on **biofilms** related to infections and implants.

With **rising demand for compact circuits**, the use of microscopes for **imaging and manipulating molecules** anchors the advancement toward **nanotechnology**, where precision control at the molecular level intersects both **microscopy** and **materials science**.
**Acoustic Microscopy** is a **technology** that uses **sound waves** to produce **images** with **microscopic resolutions**.
Initially pioneered by **Sergei Y. Sokolov** in the 1920s, acoustic waves were explored for detecting flaws in metals due to their ability to penetrate **materials opaque** to light.
Later advancements allowed these waves to be used in a reflective microscopy setting.
Scanning acoustic microscopes (SAMs) have developed to provide **high-resolution imaging** and detect **internal defects** in various materials, including biological tissues and **opaque materials**.
This **ultrasonic technique** involves sending a **pulsed sound wave** that reflects back, providing details about **contrast in density** changes within the examined materials.
Two primary advantages of acoustic microscopy are its ability to examine **opaque materials** and produce contrast based on mechanical properties.

Practical uses extend to **medical imaging**, **non-destructive testing**, and **fetal examinations**, showcasing changes in **tissue density** with high contrasts similar to or exceeding those of X-rays.
As the technology advanced, SAMs evolved from a **transmission mode** to a **reflection mode** focusing on resolving issues of lens alignment.
Most modern SAMs use **surface waves** to image features beneath opaque surfaces.
These devices have become vital for analyzing **optically opaque materials** and applications like **quality control** in **integrated circuit manufacture**.

Acoustic microscopes provide **non-destructive inspection**, examining features such as surface **cracks**, **defects**, and **boundaries**, bridging **high resolution acoustic** methods with conventional testing.
